name: Martian Moons eXploration (MMX)
short_status: Operating as of 28 October 2026: MMX lifted off on H3 flight 10 from Tanegashima at 04:41:03 JST on 20 October 2026, which is 19:41:03 UTC on 19 October, and separated into its planned orbit about 71 minutes later. On 21 October JAXA confirmed the spacecraft was healthy and closed its initial critical operations phase, moving on to checks of its onboard equipment. Arrival at Mars is planned for August 2027, with at least 10 g of Phobos due on Earth in July 2031.

facts.label: Launch
facts.value: 20 October 2026 at 04:41:03 Japan Standard Time, which is 19:41:03 UTC on 19 October 2026, from the second pad of the Yoshinobu Launch Complex at the Tanegashima Space Center. JAXA reported that the rocket flew as planned and that MMX separated normally about 1 h 11 min 13 s after liftoff and was placed into its planned orbit. It flew on the day and at the time JAXA had published on 20 August 2026.

facts.label: First days in space
facts.value: MMX was programmed to find the Sun, steady itself and open its solar arrays before calling home, JAXA's MMX team explained on 26 October, so its first signal, received early on 20 October, Japan time, showed that the rocket and the spacecraft's own software had both worked. On 21 October JAXA confirmed that the critical early sequence, which covers solar array deployment, three-axis attitude control and release of the medium-gain antenna, had gone normally and that the spacecraft was healthy, and it closed the initial critical operations phase. It then moved on to initial checks of the onboard equipment, alongside preparations for the cruise to Mars.

facts.label: Rocket
facts.value: H3 flight number 10, in the H3-24L configuration: two LE-9 first-stage engines, four SRB-3 solid boosters and the long fairing. About 63 m tall and about 575 tonnes at liftoff excluding the payload. Mitsubishi Heavy Industries is the rocket's prime contractor, and JAXA conducted the launch. JAXA's press kit for the flight calls it the H3's first planetary exploration launch and the first flight of the H3-24L.

facts.label: Ascent profile
facts.value: JAXA's plan for a 20 October launch: solid booster pairs off at 1 min 56 s and 1 min 58 s, fairing at 3 min 17 s, first-stage cutoff at 4 min 52 s, second-stage first burn from 5 min 12 s to 10 min 40 s, a coast, then a second burn from 1 h 03 min 57 s to 1 h 10 min 21 s, and separation of MMX into the planned Mars transfer orbit at 1 h 11 min 12 s, at 592 km altitude and 11.2 km/s inertial velocity. MMX flew on that date, and JAXA's launch report puts separation at about 1 h 11 min 13 s.

facts.label: Spacecraft
facts.value: Three modules: an outward propulsion module, an exploration module that does the Phobos work, and a return module. Mass figures disagree by source. JAXA's own August 2026 launch plan gives a launch mass of 4,480 kg, of which 3,030 kg is chemical propellant according to Japan's science ministry (26 August 2026), while the JPL Horizons record (revised 22 October 2026) splits the same 4,480 kg into 2,100 kg dry and 2,380 kg propellant; ESA's factsheet says about 4,200 kg including fuel. Planned mission duration five years.

facts.label: The sample
facts.value: At least 10 g of Phobos material, collected by two systems: C-SMP, a corer designed to sample from 2 cm or more below the surface, and P-SMP, a pneumatic sampler that blows regolith loose with pressurised gas and is listed as NASA-supplied in JAXA's own launch plan. JAXA's September 2026 press kit plans two landings, with the IDEFIX rover the first to touch down on Phobos.

facts.label: Payload
facts.value: JAXA's launch plan lists: TENGOO telescopic camera, OROCHI wide-angle spectral camera, MIRS near-infrared spectrometer (CNES), MEGANE gamma-ray and neutron spectrometer (listed by JAXA as NASA-provided), a laser altimeter, CMDM dust monitor, MSA ion energy mass analyser, the IDEFIX rover (CNES and DLR), the C-SMP and P-SMP samplers, the sample return capsule, an interplanetary radiation monitor, and the SHV high-definition camera, which shoots in 4K and 8K.

facts.label: IDEFIX
facts.value: A small four-wheeled rover built by CNES and DLR, to be dropped from between 40 and 100 m above Phobos, expected to bounce, then right itself and drive in gravity about a two-thousandth of Earth's. English Wikipedia gives 23.47 kg dry with a 2.44 kg payload and a body of 231 by 376 by 415 mm; European Spaceflight reported it as 25 kg when it arrived in Japan. It carries the RAX Raman spectrometer, the miniRAD radiometer, two navigation cameras and two downward-looking wheel cameras, and is designed for at least 100 days of surface work.

facts.label: Quasi-satellite orbits
facts.value: Phobos and Deimos are far too small to hold a spacecraft in a conventional orbit, so MMX flies quasi-satellite orbits: Mars-centred paths tuned so that, seen from the moon, the spacecraft appears to loop around it and stays close for long periods. ESA's factsheet describes about three years of operations around Phobos.

facts.label: Phobos, the target
facts.value: JPL Horizons (record revised 2 June 2025) gives Phobos radii of 13.1 by 11.1 by 9.3 km, a geometric albedo of 0.06, a density of 1.90 plus or minus 0.08 g/cm3, a semi-major axis of 9,377.2 km, an orbital period of 0.319 days and an inclination of 1.082 degrees. That low density, and that very dark surface, are exactly why the origin question is unresolved.

facts.label: Deimos, the secondary target
facts.value: Horizons gives Deimos radii of 7.8 by 6.0 by 5.1 km, albedo 0.06, density 1.76 plus or minus 0.30 g/cm3, semi-major axis 23,463.2 km and a period of 1.263 days. MMX is to make several Deimos flybys after leaving Phobos and before departing Mars.

facts.label: Coming home
facts.value: The return module carries a sample return capsule about 60 cm across with its own heat shield. It is to re-enter and land in Australia, after which the sample goes to JAXA's Institute of Space and Astronautical Science. JAXA's launch plan states the goal as sample return in Japanese fiscal 2031, which runs April 2031 to March 2032.

facts.label: ESA's contribution
facts.value: Deep space communication hardware, specifically a transponder and power amplifier, plus ground station support from ESA's Estrack network.

facts.label: Schedule history
facts.value: Approved for full development on 19 February 2020, then targeting a September 2024 launch, Mars orbit in August 2025, Mars departure in 2028 and Earth return in 2029. The mission slipped two years to 2026, reported on 6 December 2023, in the wake of delays to the H3 rocket it depends on. It launched on 20 October 2026, and a Japanese science ministry document of 26 August 2026 gives Mars arrival in August 2027 and Earth return in July 2031.

facts.label: Shipping to Tanegashima
facts.value: The spacecraft left Kamakura early on 28 March 2026, travelled by dedicated ship to Shimama Port on Tanegashima, arriving on 31 March 2026, and then moved to the second Spacecraft Test and Assembly Building (STA2) at the Tanegashima Space Center for system protoflight testing. The IDEFIX rover had been delivered from Europe to Japan in February 2024.

facts.label: In JPL Horizons
facts.value: JPL Horizons carries MMX as spacecraft -239. Its record, revised on 22 October 2026, lists launch at 19:41:03 UTC on 19 October 2026 and Mars arrival in August 2027. Its trajectory is JAXA's post-launch solution, built from tracking data up to 20 October and predicted from there to 2 December 2026. On that trajectory MMX is about 2.5 million km from Earth at midday UTC on 28 October 2026, moving away at about 3.2 km/s.

facts.label: JAXA's own framing
facts.value: The launch plan states the aim as achieving humanity's first sample return from the Martian sphere in fiscal 2031, and positions MMX as Japan's first move into the Mars system, gathering detailed surface, subsurface and environmental data on a moon regarded as a possible orbital staging point for future human Mars exploration. That is JAXA's description of its own mission, written in August 2026.

timeline: JAXA and Japanese government officials approve MMX to enter full development, then aiming at a September 2024 launch, Mars orbit in August 2025 and an Earth return in 2029.
The two-year slip is reported: MMX will not make the 2024 Mars window and moves to 2026, pushing the sample return from 2029 to 2031.
The Franco-German IDEFIX rover arrives in Japan from Europe for integration with the spacecraft.
The completed spacecraft departs Kamakura in the early morning aboard a dedicated ship bound for Tanegashima.
MMX arrives by ship at Shimama Port on Tanegashima, then moves to the Tanegashima Space Center's second Spacecraft Test and Assembly Building for protoflight testing.
JAXA publishes the launch schedule: 20 October 2026 at 04:41:03 Japan time on H3 flight 10, with a reserve period from 21 October to 7 November.
JAXA confirms the launch time, 04:41:03 Japan time on 20 October (19:41:03 UTC on 19 October), and extends the reserve period to 9 November.

MMX lifts off at 04:41:03 Japan time (19:41:03 UTC on 19 October) on H3 flight 10 from Tanegashima. About 1 h 11 min 13 s later the rocket releases it into its planned orbit, which JAXA's launch plan names as a Mars transfer orbit. At the post-launch press conference, mission leader Yasuhiro Kawakatsu says the spacecraft is stable, Jiji Press reports.

JAXA confirms that the critical early sequence, from deploying the solar arrays to establishing three-axis attitude and freeing the medium-gain antenna, has gone normally and that the spacecraft is healthy. It closes the initial critical operations phase and moves on to checking the onboard equipment while preparing for the cruise to Mars.
Planned: arrival in the Mars system in August 2027 (Japan's science ministry, 26 August 2026), then quasi-satellite orbits around Phobos and remote observation of both moons.

Planned, though sources disagree on the year. ESA (13 October 2026) puts the IDEFIX rover's release in early 2029, and DLR its landing in 2029 on its project page (read 28 October 2026) and around the turn of 2028 to 2029 in its launch release of 19 October 2026. For the sampling landing, ESA says 2030, NASA (15 October 2026) no earlier than 2028 and Jiji Press (20 October 2026) 2029. JAXA's press kit plans two landings and gives no year.
Planned: after sampling, MMX leaves Phobos, makes several flybys of Deimos, and departs the Mars system in November 2030, per Japan's science ministry.

Planned: the return module releases a 60 cm sample capsule that re-enters and lands in Australia, delivering at least 10 g of Phobos. JAXA states the goal as Japanese fiscal 2031, and Japan's science ministry gives July 2031.

images.caption: H3 flight 10 climbing into a dark sky on a long, bright exhaust plume, seen from below, with the core stage and its solid rocket boosters at the head of the flame and lit exhaust clouds along the bottom.

The whole H3 rocket rising off the pad at night, its orange core stage and white boosters lit by the flame, with the red and white lightning towers to the left, the umbilical tower to the right and exhaust clouds spreading along the ground.
The MMX spacecraft on a stand in a clean room, wrapped in gold thermal blanket, with a silver solar panel folded against its side, a dish antenna and dark struts folded above it.
H3 flight 10 rising on its exhaust plume above the launch pad at night, seen across the water, with the lit Vehicle Assembly Building at left and the ground cloud spreading to the right.

Close-up of the H3 flight 10 fairing with the MMX emblem large and sharp, the top of the core stage, and the red and white lightning towers and umbilical mast of the launch pad under a clear blue sky.

American and Japanese team members gathered around the gamma ray spectrometer part of MEGANE, the NASA-provided instrument that will measure the elemental composition of Phobos, during its development at the Johns Hopkins Applied Physics Laboratory.
The landing gear on a half-scale model of the MMX spacecraft displayed in the first floor atrium at the Japan Aerospace 2024 exhibition, Tokyo Big Sight, on 19 October 2024.
